newsitem.title: ROMANIA: Religion weighs upon Romanian presidential battle.
newsitem.headline: Religion weighs upon Romanian presidential battle.

text.p: Romania's Orthodox church, still reeling from the repressions of five decades of Communism, has been dragged into this week's hotly contested presidential election.
Incumbent Ion Iliescu and centrist challenger Emil Constantinescu have gone out of their way to be photographed attending crowded services.
Both praise the church, which holds the allegiance of 86 percent of Romanians, as a mainstay of post-Communist society.

Their fervour reached heights last month when they took turns visiting relics said to be those of apostle Andrew flown in from Greece to a ceremony attended by hundreds of thousands of pilgrims in the northeastern city of Iasi.
As the campaign drew to a close, the ex-communist Iliescu stood by his moral beliefs when asked bluntly by his rival during a television debate whether he believed in God.

"I was baptised in the Romanian Orthodox church but during my intellectual development there have been certain changes... Iliescu said. "I am much more a Christian than others who use their faith for campaign purposes."
Constantinescu, who describes himself as "a simple Orthodox believer", snapped back: "When were you lying? Before, when you said you were a 'free thinker', or just now?"
Though it allows its clergy to marry, the Orthodox church is inherently conservative, asking parliament earlier this year, for instance, to brand homosexuality as a crime.
Guidelines in February told parishioners to vote in elections for candidates blending faith in God and democratic commitment with tolerance and the fight against communism.
The church also asked clerics to choose politics or their ministry - not an easy line to draw in the post-communist era.

Scandal engulfed the church after Iliescu's leftist Party of Social Democracy (PDSR) was trounced by the opposition in this month's parliamentary polls and thrown out of government for the first time since the 1989 fall of communism.

A senior cleric within the PDSR read out a letter in parliament announcing that the head of the Orthodox church, Patriarch Teoctist, had been removed in a plot hatched by priests close to the opposition.
The letter turned out to be a hoax.
But each presidential finalist used it to accuse the other of being behind an "attempt to destabilise the church".
Communism stripped the church of much of its property and jailed some 2,000 Orthodox priests, along with clerics of minority faiths -- Roman and Greek Catholics and Protestants.

"Over the past seven years there have been significant steps to bring the missionary activity of the Orthodox church back to normal," said church spokesman Bishop Teofan Sinaitul. "But the road to normality is still long."

Teoctist's ornate patriarchate building miraculously escaped the demolition of one-third of old Bucharest ordered by late dictator Nicolae Ceausescu to make way for a megalomaniac palace to his own glory.
Before his execution in a 1989 popular upheaval, Ceausescu bulldozed or moved out of sight hundreds of churches throughout the country to erect mammoth public buildings.
Many priests were forced to bow to Ceausescu's whims during his 24-year rule and now make amends by seeking a role in public service.
"What the church wants is for the state to return its confiscated property so that it can resume its role within Romanian society," Bishop Teofan said.
